Capital One just announced it’s acquiring Brex for $5.15 billion.  An incredible, top 0.1% “exit” in less than 10 years from a category creator that created massive wealth and opportunities.  A huge win.
But also … less than half of Brex’s $12.3 billion valuation from October 2022.
Should anyone care?  Many are seeing is a failure vs Ramp, a measured success at best.  But … why?
I don’t think most people commenting on this actually understand what they’re reacting to. What they’re really feeling—even if they can’t articulate it—is the consequences of
hubristic fundraising
.
And we should probably talk about it. Because hubristic fundraising is back. In a big way. It was back big time in 2025 and is back even bigger time in 2026.

Let me define it simply: Hubristic fundraising is when you raise at a valuation so aggressive, with terms so favorable, with a narrative so bold, that you are essentially betting the entire future of your company on hitting an extraordinary outcome.
It’s not just “raising a lot of money.” Plenty of companies raise hundreds of millions without hubris.
Hubristic fundraising is when you:
Take a valuation that requires Top 0.1%+ annual growth for a decade to grow into
Raise at 100x-500x+ revenue multiple.  Often, again and again.
Build your entire talent acquisition, press strategy, and customer pitch around being “the most valuable” or “fastest-growing”
Create expectations that anything less than a $20B+ IPO or massive strategic exit is a disappointment

So I’ve been doing quite a bit of speaking and mentoring lately on what we should expect going forward re: AI in B2B / SaaS. One thing many speakers emphasize (and also many founders) is you have to make your app much more personal. That everyone will want an agent … and one that knows them, and how they use the app. And while I think there is some truth here — personally I don’t know if every interaction has to be like this:
I can see why folks might feel that way. But honestly I’m not sure. A related point is if you want to truly delight customers these days, you probably do need to go multi-product. Not just offer additional products. But really deeply understand how they interact across multiple products. And again, maybe personalize those interactions. Because otherwise, you’ll miss opportunities to improve workflows that span multiple products. There are so many great examples of this now. HubSpot is perhaps the #1 example. They now sell 10+ products. You could argue almost all of us now sell 3-4 core apps. The key is HubSpot does deep workflow mapping across their entire platform. So when you ask it anything, it knows which products you’re using, and builds solutions based on >all< those products together. It’s incredible. Another vendor I love that does this well is Gong. In fact, my favorite AI VP of Marketing ever told me she uses Gong because Gong ties into Marketo and Salesforce automatically. She never had to log in herself. No matter where she went in the application. The agent knew her data. That’s powerful. And it seems to me, both examples are “personalized” in that they map out exactly what each individual account does, what agents and humans are doing, and tie it all together in real-time.

So we've had some interesting discussions on LinkedIn and X about who does what in AI, and how much personalization there has to be, etc. The latest one was "Who said that AI means everything in SaaS needs to be a personalized experience?"
I think it was Anneka Gupta, CEO of Asana. So I don't know if she said that or not, but it makes sense given her background. She came out of Twilio, so maybe it should have been obvious when I met her, that she would say that. But then also, being the head of developer experience before taking over as CEO. So perhaps that's where that comes from.
And just my learnings from being an investor since 2010. It seems like no matter what people tell us -- they're telling us something different now than ever before. They told us the future is multi-product. Now they're saying it's single product because nobody wants to buy anything else anymore. We were told the future is agentic. Then they're saying the future is more humans working harder. People change their minds on these topics every two years. It's hard to keep track. So, you gotta make your mind up on these things.
But if I'm right, then the thing that will accelerate is going to be customers demanding more value per seat. That's probably always true. You want more value per employee. And so you're gonna see a lot more efficiency. There's already a lot of movement towards agents replacing humans and even software replacing humans. And so I think that trend will continue. A good example, Asana's NRR didn't go down during the downturn, which is unusual. And the number one driver was driving up the ACV by 25%. That was the big driver of accelerating revenue at scale for them. Not new logo acquisition.
